meaning: Shows you are willing to go to extreme or unusual lengths to reach a goal: “even if it means ...”, “even at the cost of ...”.
connection: Verb te-form + でも (followed by an expression of will, wish or determination)

senses.label: Whatever it takes
senses.meaning: Shows you will reach a goal even by drastic means. The first part is a step most people would rather avoid. The second part is usually a will or duty expression such as 「〜たい」, 「〜つもりだ」 or 「〜なければならない」.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + でも + 〜たい／〜つもりだ／〜する
examples: I want to buy this house, even if I have to borrow money.
I'll finish the report by tomorrow, even if I have to stay up all night.
I plan to go to my child's recital, even if it means taking a day off work.

senses.label: 何としてでも (no matter what)
senses.meaning: The set phrases 「何としてでも」 and 「どうしてでも」 mean “no matter what”, “by any means”. They are strong and show firm determination.
senses.connection: 何として／どうして + でも + expression of will
examples: I want to win the match no matter what.
This one promise I will keep, no matter what.

notes: The second part must be the speaker's will, wish, resolve or claim. It cannot be a plain objective fact.
The first part is usually a costly step people would normally avoid. This gives the strong “at any cost” tone.
Don't confuse it with 「〜ても」 (even if). 「〜ても」 is a simple concession; 「〜てでも」 stresses being ready to take that step to reach a goal.

daily.title: Talking about your dream
daily.description: Telling a friend about something you really want to achieve.
daily.example: I want to study abroad, even if I have to take on more part-time work.

daily.title: Getting concert tickets
daily.description: A friend says they will pay any price to see a concert.
daily.example: I want to get tickets for that concert, even if I have to wait in line.

daily.title: Making a family member see a doctor
daily.description: A family member refuses to go to the hospital, and you insist.
daily.example: I'll take you to the hospital even if I have to drag you there.

work.title: Rushing a project
work.description: The project lead tells the team the deadline will be met.
work.example: We'll meet the delivery date, even if we have to work on our days off.

work.title: Winning a client
work.description: A salesperson shows determination to close a deal.
work.example: We want to win this contract no matter what.

etymology: Formed from the verb te-form plus the particle 「でも」. 「でも」 means “even”, so together they stress “even taking this step, (I will reach my goal)”. In 「何としてでも」, 「として」 is the te-form of 「とする」.

similar.title: 〜まで(して)・〜てまで
similar.explanation: Both mean going to great lengths. 「〜てまで」 often carries criticism or disapproval, as in 「人をだましてまで金をもうけたくない」 (I don't want to make money if it means deceiving people). 「〜てでも」 usually expresses your own resolve and sounds more positive.

similar.title: 〜ても (even if)
similar.explanation: 「〜ても」 is just a concession: even if the first part is true, the result stays the same, as in 「雨が降っても行く」. With 「〜てでも」, the first part is a step you choose to take on purpose to reach a goal.

similar.title: 〜てまで／〜までして
similar.explanation: An N1 pattern that is stronger and often criticizes someone for “going that far”. 「〜てでも」 states your resolve positively, and the second part is usually a will expression.

meaning: Shows that the situation is urgent or you feel restless, so you can't stay in a certain state any longer: “I can't keep ...ing”, “I can't afford to ...”.
connection: Verb te-form + は + いられない (casual: 〜ちゃいられない)

senses.label: Can't keep doing
senses.meaning: The situation is pressing, so you can't relax and stay as you are. It often sounds impatient, like urging yourself on. Typical verbs describe a state: 「のんびりする」, 「じっとする」, 「待つ」, 「寝る」.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + はいられない／はいられません
examples: The exam is only a week away. I can't take it easy anymore.
We can't rest in a place like this. Let's hurry on.
I can't wait any longer.

senses.label: Can't stay calm / can't sit still
senses.meaning: Your feelings are too strong to stay calm or silent: 「黙ってはいられない」 (can't keep quiet), 「じっとしてはいられない」 (can't sit still). Often used when you see something unfair or worrying.
senses.connection: 黙って／じっとして／落ち着いて + はいられない
examples: After hearing such an awful story, I can't keep quiet.
My daughter hadn't come home, and I was too worried to sit still.
I can't just sit here. Let's go right now.

notes: In speech, 「ては」 often becomes 「ちゃ」 and 「では」 becomes 「じゃ」: 「寝ちゃいられない」, 「休んじゃいられない」.
「いられない」 is the negative potential of 「いる」. The kanji spelling 「居られない」 is rare.
Don't confuse it with 「〜ないではいられない」 (can't help doing), which is built on the negative form + ではいられない.

daily.title: Seeing others make progress
daily.description: Your friends are working hard, so you can't fall behind.
daily.example: Everyone's working so hard. I can't let myself lose either.

daily.title: Oversleeping
daily.description: The alarm has gone off several times, and you must get up now.
daily.example: It's already eight! I can't stay in bed.

daily.title: A family member is ill
daily.description: You hear a family member is in the hospital and want to rush over.
daily.example: After hearing that, I can't just sit still.

work.title: A rival launches a new product
work.description: In a department meeting, someone stresses the need to act fast.
work.example: Now that another company has released a new product, we can't just stand by and watch.

work.title: A deadline approaches
work.description: The boss reminds the team to hurry.
work.example: The deadline is next week. We can't afford to take our time.

etymology: The 「いる」 of 「〜ている」 becomes the negative potential 「いられない」, and the topic particle 「は」 is inserted after the te-form. The literal sense is “can't remain in the state of ...”, which extended to “things are urgent, so I can't go on ...”.

similar.title: 〜てばかりはいられない
similar.explanation: Adding 「ばかり」 gives “can't just keep ...ing”. It admits the first part is understandable, but you can't do only that. 「〜てはいられない」 means you can't continue the state at all, and it sounds more urgent.

similar.title: 〜ないではいられない
similar.explanation: Follows the negative form and means “can't help doing”, as in 「笑わないではいられない」. 「〜てはいられない」 follows the affirmative te-form and means “can't stay in this state”.

similar.title: 〜ている場合じゃない
similar.explanation: A close colloquial equivalent: “this is no time to ...”. It stresses that the timing is wrong. 「〜てはいられない」 focuses more on the speaker's inner impatience.

meaning: Shows that, understandable as it is, you can't just keep doing one thing or staying in one state: “can't just keep ...ing”.
connection: Verb te-form + ばかりはいられない (also 〜てばかりもいられない)

senses.label: Can't just keep doing
senses.meaning: You can't keep doing only this. Something has to change, or you have to act. Often used to motivate yourself: “I can't go on like this”. Typical verbs: 「泣く」, 「悲しむ」, 「遊ぶ」, 「休む」.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + ばかりはいられない／ばかりもいられない
examples: I can't keep crying forever. Let's look ahead.
I can't just keep regretting my failure.
I can't keep relying on my parents.

senses.label: Can't just be happy
senses.meaning: The first part can also be something positive, such as 「喜ぶ」 or 「安心する」. It means “we can't just celebrate; there are still problems ahead”. The tone is calm and cautionary.
senses.connection: 喜んで／安心して／笑って + ばかりはいられない
examples: I passed, but I can't just celebrate. The real work starts after I enroll.
Sales have grown, but we can't relax just yet.

notes: Both 「ばかりは」 and 「ばかりも」 are common. 「も」 sounds a little softer.
It is the opposite of 「〜てばかりいる」 (always ...ing). This pattern denies that state: you can't keep going like that.
In speech you can also say 「〜てばっかりもいられない」.

daily.title: Bouncing back after a breakup
daily.description: After a breakup, a friend encourages herself to start again.
daily.example: I can't keep moping. Starting tomorrow, I'll do my best again.

daily.title: The end of summer vacation
daily.description: A student realizes it's time to stop just having fun.
daily.example: Summer vacation is almost over. I can't just keep playing.

work.title: A results meeting
work.description: Business has improved, but the president warns against relaxing.
work.example: Our results have recovered, but we're not in a position to just celebrate.

work.title: News commentary
work.description: A commentator discusses a social problem and calls for action.
work.example: We can't just keep waiting for the government to act. We should think about what our community can do.

etymology: Built from 「〜てばかりいる」 (always ...ing) plus the particle 「は／も」, with 「いる」 changed to the negative potential 「いられない」. Literally, “can't remain in the state of always ...ing”.

similar.title: 〜てはいられない
similar.explanation: 「〜てはいられない」 means you can't keep up the state at all, and it is more urgent. 「〜てばかりはいられない」 admits the first part is understandable, but you can't do “only” that.

similar.title: 〜てばかりいる
similar.explanation: 「〜てばかりいる」 describes the current state of “always ...ing”, often critically. This pattern denies that state: “I can't keep doing that”.

similar.title: 〜ている場合じゃない
similar.explanation: Colloquial: “this is no time to ...”. It stresses that the timing is wrong and things are urgent.

meaning: Gives permission or says something is acceptable: “it's fine to ...”, “there's no problem with ...”. More formal than 「〜てもいい」.
connection: Verb te-form／i-adjective くて／na-adjective or noun で + も差し支えない

senses.label: Permission / no problem
senses.meaning: Says that doing something causes no problem and is allowed. It is a formal version of 「〜てもいい」 and 「〜てもかまわない」. Used in business, official documents, instructions and other formal settings.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + も差し支えない／も差し支えありません
examples: You may fill out this form in pencil.
It's fine to join the meeting a little late.
If it's tomorrow, you are welcome to call us.

senses.label: Acceptable condition
senses.meaning: After nouns or adjectives, it means “even ... is acceptable”. It loosens a condition or shows how far you can compromise.
senses.connection: Noun／na-adjective + でも差し支えない; i-adjective くて + も差し支えない
examples: If the person cannot come in person, a representative is also acceptable.
I don't mind if it's a bit old. Could you let me have your computer?

notes: 「差し支え」 means “hindrance, inconvenience”, so 「差し支えない」 means “there is no hindrance”.
Politeness scale: 〜てもいい < 〜てもかまわない < 〜ても差し支えない. With superiors or clients, use 「差し支えありません／ございません」.
「差し支えなければ」 is a polite set phrase meaning “if you don't mind”. It is used for requests, not for giving permission.
You can drop 「も」 and say 「〜て差し支えない」 with the same meaning.

daily.title: At the doctor's
daily.description: The doctor tells a patient what they can do.
daily.example: You can take a bath starting today.

daily.title: Filling out an application
daily.description: A staff member explains how to fill in the form.
daily.example: You may write the reading in hiragana.

work.title: Answering a client's question
work.description: A client asks if a delay is possible, and the person in charge replies formally.
work.example: It is perfectly fine if the delivery is next week.

work.title: Explaining company rules
work.description: HR explains the dress code.
work.example: In summer, you are not required to wear a jacket.

work.title: Arranging a meeting
work.description: The boss says you can skip part of the agenda.
work.example: You don't need to attend the second half of the agenda.

etymology: 「差し支える」 means “to be hindered, to cause trouble”. It combines the prefix 「差し」 with 「支える」 (to get stuck, to be blocked). Its noun form 「差し支え」 plus 「ない」 means “no hindrance”, and with 「〜ても」 it means “even if ..., there is no hindrance”.

similar.title: 〜てもいい
similar.explanation: The most common way to give permission, used in both speech and writing. 「〜ても差し支えない」 is more formal and appears mostly in business and official documents.

similar.title: 〜てもかまわない
similar.explanation: In the middle on the politeness scale: “I don't mind if ...”. 「〜ても差し支えない」 sounds more objective and formal, and is common in explanations and replies to clients.

similar.title: 差し支えなければ
similar.explanation: A polite set phrase meaning “if you don't mind”, used when asking someone to do something, as in 「差し支えなければ、お名前を伺えますか」. It does not give permission.

meaning: (1) To show someone how to do something, to demonstrate. (2) The speaker's strong determination: “I'll show you I can ...”.
connection: Verb te-form + みせる (the kanji 「見せる」 is rarely used here)

senses.label: Demonstrate
senses.meaning: To actually do something so the other person understands: “show how to ...”, “demonstrate”. The subject is often a teacher, senior or someone teaching others.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + みせる／みせた／みせてくれる
examples: The teacher actually swam to show us how.
My mother slowly demonstrated the steps of the recipe.
The clerk explained how to use it while showing us how it worked.

senses.label: Determination
senses.meaning: The speaker announces strong resolve to others: “I'll do it, just watch”. Usually in the non-past 「〜てみせる」, often with 「必ず」, 「きっと」 or 「絶対」. It has a refusing-to-lose tone.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + みせる (often with 「必ず」 or 「絶対に」)
examples: This time I'll pass for sure, you'll see.
I will definitely win the championship.
No matter how hard it is, I'll get it done, just watch.

senses.label: Put on a show
senses.meaning: To deliberately put on a certain look or attitude for others, not meaning it. For example, 「笑ってみせる」 means “force a smile”.
senses.connection: 笑って／平気な顔をして + みせる
examples: She put on a smile so no one would worry.

notes: For determination, the subject is first person, usually in the non-past 「〜てみせる」. When speaking to others, use 「〜てみせます」.
Don't confuse it with 「〜てみる」 (try doing). 「〜てみる」 is trying something yourself; 「〜てみせる」 is doing it for others to see.
As an auxiliary it is usually written in kana 「みせる」. The kanji 「見せる」 usually means literally showing someone an object.

daily.title: Making a bold claim to a friend
daily.description: A friend doesn't believe you can lose weight.
daily.example: Just watch. I'll lose five kilos by summer.

daily.title: Teaching a child
daily.description: A father shows his child how to tie shoelaces.
daily.example: OK, Daddy will show you how.

daily.title: Before a match
daily.description: An athlete states their resolve in a pre-game interview.
daily.example: I'll win the next match, you'll see.

work.title: Training new staff
work.description: A senior colleague demonstrates a task to new employees.
work.example: First I'll enter it once to show you, so please watch carefully.

work.title: Taking on a tough project
work.description: The person in charge shows their resolve to the boss.
work.example: I will make this project a success, I promise.

etymology: Formed from the verb te-form plus 「見せる」 (to show). Literally “do it and show it”, which means demonstrating. From “doing it for someone to see” came the sense of resolve: “I'll do it and show you”. As an auxiliary verb, it is usually written in kana.

similar.title: 〜てみる
similar.explanation: 「〜てみる」 means trying something and focuses on your own result. 「〜てみせる」 means doing it for others to see, or declaring your resolve to them.

similar.title: 〜てやる (defiant resolve)
similar.explanation: 「〜てやる」 also shows resolve, but it is rougher, with a spiteful or revengeful tone, as in 「見返してやる」 (I'll show them). 「〜てみせる」 is more positive: achieving results for others to see.

similar.title: 〜つもりだ
similar.explanation: 「〜つもりだ」 simply states an intention in a flat tone. 「〜てみせる」 carries a strong will not to lose and to impress others.

title: 〜ては (repetition)
meaning: Shows two actions alternating or repeating: “do A, then B, then A again ...”, “every time A, B”.
connection: Verb te-form + は + verb (often as 「〜ては〜、〜ては〜」)

senses.label: Back and forth
senses.meaning: Two actions alternate and repeat many times. Often written twice: 「AてはB、AてはB」. It usually describes pointless or monotonous repetition.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + は + verb masu-stem, verb te-form + は + verb masu-stem
examples: I wrote and erased, wrote and erased, and finally finished the letter.
The rain keeps starting and stopping, starting and stopping.
The baby keeps falling asleep and waking up, and crying when she wakes.

senses.label: Every time A, B
senses.meaning: Every time A happens, B follows, forming a habit: “whenever ..., ...”. The second part often shows the speaker's resignation or criticism.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + は + verb (the second part is often in the ta-form or ている form)
examples: Whenever my father drinks, he talks about the old days.
Whenever he had time off, he went climbing in the mountains alone.
As a child, I often got into fights with friends and then got scolded by my mother.

notes: Mostly used in writing and narratives. It is less common in conversation.
It has the same form as the negative-condition 「〜ては」 (「そんなに食べては太るよ」). Look at the second part: if it is a repeated action, it is this usage.
After 「〜ては」 you can use the masu-stem to link clauses, as in 「食べては寝、食べては寝」.

daily.title: Reading a novel
daily.description: A novel describes the main character's hesitation.
daily.example: She picked up the phone and put it down, picked it up and put it down.

daily.title: Complaining about a lazy holiday
daily.description: Telling a friend how you wasted a long weekend.
daily.example: During the holidays, all I did was eat and sleep.

daily.title: Childhood memories
daily.description: Chatting with family about when you were little.
daily.example: I used to play by the river and come home with my clothes all dirty.

work.title: Reporting on development
work.description: An engineer explains a process of trial and error.
work.example: We built prototypes and improved them, over and over again.

work.title: Essays and reports
work.description: A reporter describes the hard rebuilding of a disaster area.
work.example: Houses were built and destroyed, built and destroyed, yet the residents never gave up hope.

etymology: Formed from the verb te-form plus the topic particle 「は」. 「は」 marks the first part as one “event unit” and links it to the next, so repeating it creates the rhythm of an action happening again and again.

similar.title: 〜たり〜たりする
similar.explanation: 「〜たり〜たり」 can also show alternation (「行ったり来たり」, going back and forth), but it simply lists actions without stressing a cycle. 「〜ては〜」 stresses the same process repeating, often in vain.

similar.title: 〜ては・〜では (bad result)
similar.explanation: Same form, but it means “if ..., (something bad) will happen”, as in 「そんなに休んでは困る」. In this pattern, the second part is an action that actually repeats.

similar.title: 〜たびに
similar.explanation: 「〜たびに」 clearly means “every time ...” and sounds objective. 「〜ては」 is more literary and often paints a habit or a repeated scene.

meaning: The speaker's judgment on the true nature of something: “that's what ... is”, “that's just ...”.
connection: Noun／verb or adjective plain form + というものだ (na-adjectives and nouns usually drop 「だ」)

senses.label: True nature
senses.meaning: Based on common sense, the speaker declares that this is the essence of something: “that's what ... is all about”. Often used when reflecting or stating a principle.
senses.connection: Noun + というものだ (e.g. 「これが人生というものだ」)
examples: Things not going as planned: that's life.
Helping each other in hard times: that's true friendship.
That's what a parent's love is, isn't it?

senses.label: Evaluation / criticism
senses.meaning: Evaluates someone else's words or actions, usually critically: “that's just ...”. Often follows evaluative words like 「無理」, 「わがまま」, 「迷惑」 or 「当然」.
senses.connection: Plain form + というものだ／というものではないか
examples: Finishing this much in one day? That's simply impossible.
Making a loud racket in the middle of the night is a nuisance to the neighbors.
After working this hard, isn't it only natural to pass?

notes: Mostly used in writing or serious discussion. In speech, people often say 「〜ってもんだ」.
The negative 「〜というものではない」 has a completely different meaning (“it's not true that ... is enough”) and is a separate grammar point.
「〜というものだ」 is the speaker's own judgment. It is not used to report what others said.

daily.title: Comforting a friend
daily.description: A friend complains about work, and you say it happens to everyone.
daily.example: Well, learning from your mistakes is what being young is all about.

daily.title: Reacting to a demand
daily.description: A friend asks too much, and you're annoyed.
daily.example: Telling me to answer by today? That's just selfish.

daily.title: Reading an essay
daily.description: The writer talks about the meaning of travel.
daily.example: Walking through a town you don't know: that is the real joy of travel.

work.title: Raising an objection in a meeting
work.description: An employee objects to an unreasonable demand.
work.example: Finishing this in three months on this budget is simply impossible.

work.title: Newspaper editorial
work.description: An editorial criticizes the government.
work.example: Raising taxes without explaining it to the public is simply dishonest.

etymology: Made of the quoting 「という」, the formal noun 「もの」 and the copula 「だ」. 「もの」 refers to the nature or general character of things, so 「というものだ」 means “that is the thing called ... (that's just how it is)”, which became the speaker's judgment about the nature of something.

similar.title: 〜というものではない
similar.explanation: The negative has a different meaning: “it's not true that ... is all it takes”. It rejects a one-sided view, as in 「高ければいいというものではない」 (expensive doesn't automatically mean good).

similar.title: 〜ものだ (common sense / feelings)
similar.explanation: 「〜ものだ」 states a general truth or a feeling, as in 「人は変わるものだ」 (people change). 「〜というものだ」 has a defining sense (“what is called ...”) and stresses judgment and evaluation.

similar.title: 〜にほかならない
similar.explanation: Means “is nothing other than ...”. It stresses a cause or essence and sounds more formal and forceful.

meaning: Rejects a one-sided view: “it's not true that ... is all it takes”, “... doesn't necessarily ...”.
connection: Verb or adjective plain form／noun + というものではない (also 〜というものでもない)

senses.label: Not enough just to ...
senses.meaning: Rejects the simple idea that “as long as ..., it's fine”. The first part is often 「〜ばいい」, 「〜たらいい」 or 「〜さえすれば」. The tone is gentle but firm, used for reasoning or giving advice.
senses.connection: 〜ばいい／〜たらいい + というものではない
examples: Taking a lot of medicine doesn't make it work better.
Studying isn't just about putting in long hours.
You can't fix this just by saying sorry.

senses.label: Not necessarily
senses.meaning: A statement does not always hold true: “it's not necessarily the case that ...”. Often used with 「必ずしも」 or 「誰でも」. 「〜というものでもない」 sounds softer.
senses.connection: Plain form + というものではない／というものでもない
examples: Just because something is expensive doesn't mean it's good quality.
Having talent doesn't mean anyone will succeed.

notes: Colloquial forms include 「〜というもんじゃない」 and 「〜ってもんじゃない」.
「〜というものでもない」 is softer than 「〜というものではない」: “not necessarily”.
Often paired with 「〜からといって」: “just because ..., it doesn't necessarily ...”.

daily.title: Advising a dieting friend
daily.description: A friend plans to lose weight just by not eating, and you suggest a better way.
daily.example: Not eating isn't enough to lose weight. You need to exercise too.

daily.title: A parent teaching a child
daily.description: A parent explains what a gift really means.
daily.example: A present isn't better just because it's expensive, you know.

work.title: Advising a team member
work.description: A boss coaches a subordinate on writing reports.
work.example: More material isn't always better. Focus on the key points.

work.title: Opinion piece
work.description: An expert comments on education policy.
work.example: Adding more class hours won't necessarily improve academic ability.

etymology: The negative of 「というものだ」 (that's what ... is). 「もの」 refers to a general nature or principle, so the negative means “by its nature, that is not how it works”, rejecting a one-sided view.

similar.title: 〜というものだ
similar.explanation: The affirmative states the essence or evaluates something, as in 「それが人生というものだ」. The negative rejects a one-sided view. They are not simple opposites.

similar.title: 〜わけではない
similar.explanation: 「〜わけではない」 denies a conclusion drawn from the situation: “it doesn't mean that ...”. 「〜というものではない」 denies a general principle or one-sided idea, and often follows 「〜ばいい」.

similar.title: 〜とは限らない
similar.explanation: 「〜とは限らない」 means “not always”, focusing on possible exceptions. 「〜というものではない」 focuses on rejecting the simple idea that “... is all it takes”.

meaning: Gives a few examples of a category: “such as ...”, “... and other ... like that”.
connection: Noun + (や) noun + といった + noun

senses.label: Listing examples
senses.meaning: Lists two or more typical examples, followed by a general noun: “... such as A and B”. It implies there are others of the same kind. More formal than 「〜など」.
senses.connection: Noun A + や／、 + noun B + といった + noun
examples: At this restaurant, you can eat Japanese food such as sushi and tempura.
Old cities like Kyoto and Nara attract many foreign tourists.
Sports such as soccer and baseball are popular.

senses.label: Summing up a type
senses.meaning: After one or more examples, 「といった」 introduces a category of similar things. Common phrases: 「〜といった感じ」 (that kind of feeling) and 「〜といったところ」 (about that much).
senses.connection: Noun or phrase + といった + 感じ／もの／こと, etc.
examples: If you get symptoms like a headache or dizziness, rest right away.
He looked as if there were no particular problems.

notes: 「といった」 must be followed by a noun that sums up the examples before it.
Don't confuse it with 「と言った」 (said). When reporting speech, 「と言った」 usually ends the sentence or is followed by other elements.
「AやBなどといった」 is also common. 「など」 and 「といった」 can be used together.

daily.title: Describing your hometown
daily.description: Telling a friend about local specialties.
daily.example: My hometown is famous for fruit like apples and grapes.

daily.title: Watching the news
daily.description: The news covers popular hobbies.
daily.example: Outdoor activities such as camping and fishing are popular these days.

daily.title: Talking about study methods
daily.description: Friends chat about ways to learn a language.
daily.example: It's also good to learn from familiar things like anime and TV dramas.

work.title: Job requirements
work.description: HR explains the skills they need.
work.example: We are looking for people who can speak foreign languages such as English or Chinese.

work.title: Product presentation
work.description: Presenting where a product can be used.
work.example: This product is suitable for large spaces such as meeting rooms and classrooms.

etymology: Formed from the quoting particle 「と」 plus 「言った」, the past form of 「言う」. Its original meaning was “called ...”. When modifying a noun, the meaning weakened to “like ...”, and it became a way to list examples. It is usually written in kana.

similar.title: 〜や〜など
similar.explanation: 「など」 can take particles and work directly in a sentence, and is used in both speech and writing. 「といった」 must be followed by a noun, sounds more formal, and suggests “this kind of thing”.

similar.title: 〜とか〜とか
similar.explanation: 「とか」 is casual and lists things loosely. 「といった」 is a more formal, written way of listing.

similar.title: 〜という (called)
similar.explanation: 「Aという + noun」 means “a ... called A”, with only one A. 「AやBといった + noun」 lists examples of the same kind.

meaning: Rejects the first part and presents something more extreme or the opposite: “far from ..., actually ...”, “not only ..., but even ...”.
connection: Noun／na-adjective stem／verb or i-adjective plain form + どころか

senses.label: Far from it, the opposite
senses.meaning: Completely rejects the first part and presents the opposite fact: “far from ..., actually ...”. The second part often goes with 「逆に」 or 「かえって」. The first part is usually what someone expected.
senses.connection: Plain form／noun + どころか、(逆に) 〜
examples: I took the medicine, but far from getting better, I got worse.
Time off? Far from it, I'm working overtime every day.
Far from apologizing, he actually got angry.

senses.label: Not only ... but even
senses.meaning: Means “not just A, but even the bigger B ...” or “not even the smaller thing is possible”. Often as 「AどころかBも／さえ〜ない」.
senses.connection: Noun or plain form + どころか + noun も／さえ + 〜ない
examples: Forget kanji, I can't even write hiragana.
She speaks not only English, but French and German too.
I'm so busy that, never mind traveling, I can't even take a walk around the neighborhood.

senses.label: それどころか (on the contrary)
senses.meaning: Used as a conjunction at the start of a sentence: “not only that, but ...”, “on the contrary ...”. It picks up the previous sentence and adds something further or opposite.
senses.connection: Start of sentence + それどころか、〜
examples: He hasn't reflected on it at all. On the contrary, he's blaming others.

notes: 「どころか」 carries a strong sense of surprise or dissatisfaction, usually when things turn out contrary to expectations.
Na-adjectives and nouns attach directly to 「どころか」, usually without 「な／の」: 「静かどころか」.
Don't confuse it with 「〜どころではない」, which means “in no position to ...”.

daily.title: Complaining about the weather
daily.description: You expected the weather to clear, but it got worse.
daily.example: Far from stopping, the rain is getting heavier.

daily.title: Talking about a diet
daily.description: Complaining to a friend that your diet failed.
daily.example: Far from losing weight, I gained three kilos.

daily.title: Praising a friend's cooking
daily.description: A friend modestly says their cooking is nothing special.
daily.example: Bad? Not at all. It tastes like restaurant food.

work.title: Results report
work.description: Reporting that a new policy didn't work as expected.
work.example: Far from improving efficiency, the new system has increased our workload.

work.title: News report
work.description: Reporting a worsening economy.
work.example: Far from recovering, the economy is getting even worse.

etymology: 「どころ」 is the voiced form of 「ところ（所）」, meaning “place, degree”. 「か」 is the question particle. The original sense was roughly “how could it be at the level of ...?”, a rhetorical question that rejects the first part and leads to something more extreme or the opposite.

similar.title: 〜ばかりか
similar.explanation: 「〜ばかりか」 adds on: “not only ..., but also ...”, and the first part is affirmed. 「〜どころか」 first rejects the first part, then gives the opposite or a more extreme case, and sounds stronger.

similar.title: 〜どころではない
similar.explanation: Means there's no room at all to do something for some reason, as in 「忙しくて旅行どころではない」. 「〜どころか」 links two parts and presents the opposite or a more extreme case.

similar.title: 〜さえ
similar.explanation: 「〜さえ」 means “even”. It often combines with 「どころか」 as 「AどころかBさえ〜ない」, and the two play different roles.

meaning: Shows that because of some situation you have no time, room or energy for something: “in no position to ...”, “... is out of the question”.
connection: Noun／verb dictionary form + どころではない (casual: 〜どころじゃない)

senses.label: No room for it
senses.meaning: You're too busy, or something too urgent is happening, to do something. The first part is usually something fun or everyday, such as 「旅行」, 「勉強」 or 「花見」. The tone is one of resignation.
senses.connection: Noun／verb dictionary form + どころではない／どころじゃない
examples: I'm so busy with work that a trip is out of the question.
I had a fever, so studying was out of the question.
The exam is tomorrow, so I'm in no position to go out and play.

senses.label: Far more than ...
senses.meaning: 「〜どころの話ではない」 and 「〜どころの騒ぎではない」 mean the reality goes far beyond the first part: “it's not just ...; it's much worse”.
senses.connection: Noun or plain form + どころの話／騒ぎではない
examples: The damage this time is way more than a million yen.
It wasn't just a little delay; the meeting was canceled.

notes: In speech, 「〜どころじゃない」 is common. The polite form is 「〜どころではありません」.
「それどころではない」 can be used alone: “I can't think about that right now”.
Don't confuse it with 「〜どころか」, which links two parts and presents the opposite or a more extreme case.

daily.title: Turning down an invitation
daily.description: A friend invites you for drinks, but you're busy moving.
daily.example: Sorry, I'm getting ready to move, so a drinking party is out of the question right now.

daily.title: Hay fever season
daily.description: It's cherry blossom season, but your hay fever is terrible.
daily.example: My hay fever is so bad that cherry blossom viewing is out of the question.

daily.title: A sick child
daily.description: Family ask about your weekend plans, and you explain.
daily.example: My kid had a fever, so I couldn't think about any of that.

work.title: Year-end rush
work.description: A coworker suggests taking time off, but you're too busy.
work.example: With the year-end closing, a vacation is out of the question.

work.title: Disaster news
work.description: A report on residents in a disaster area.
work.example: Residents of the disaster area are busy rebuilding their lives and have no room to think about the future.

etymology: 「どころ」 is the voiced form of 「ところ（所）」, meaning “occasion, point”. 「〜どころではない」 literally means “this is not the occasion for ...”, which extended to “now is not the time; I can't even think about it”.

similar.title: 〜どころか
similar.explanation: 「〜どころか」 rejects the first part and leads to the opposite or something more extreme. 「〜どころではない」 comes at the end of the sentence and means “no room to ...”.

similar.title: 〜ている場合じゃない
similar.explanation: 「〜ている場合じゃない」 stresses “I shouldn't be doing ... now”, often as a reminder to yourself. 「〜どころではない」 stresses that there is objectively no room.

similar.title: 〜ないどころではない
similar.explanation: Sometimes 「〜ないどころではない」 is used to mean “far worse than just not ...”, but it is rare. Learning the affirmative connection is usually enough.

meaning: Makes a guess based on what you can see: “judging from ..., it seems ...”.
connection: Verb or i-adjective plain form／na-adjective + な + ところを見ると

senses.label: Guessing from what you see
senses.meaning: Uses a fact you see in front of you as evidence to guess a cause or situation. The second part usually has a guessing expression: 「〜らしい」, 「〜ようだ」, 「〜に違いない」 or 「〜のだろう」.
senses.connection: Plain form + ところを見ると、〜らしい／ようだ／に違いない
examples: Judging from how he's beaming, something good must have happened.
Since there's no reply, he's probably still angry.
Judging from the line in front of the shop, it must be delicious.

senses.label: ところから見ると
senses.meaning: You can also say 「〜ところから見ると」 or 「〜ところを見れば」 with the same meaning. They sound a bit more formal and are common in writing and reasoning.
senses.connection: Plain form + ところから見ると／ところを見れば
examples: Judging from the light being off in the room, she seems to have gone to bed.
Seeing that he's keeping quiet, he's probably against it.

notes: The evidence is something concrete the speaker saw. The second part can't be the speaker's own intention or a stated fact.
It can also be written 「ところをみると」. In speech, 「〜のを見ると」 is common.
Don't confuse it with 「〜ところを見られる」 (be seen while doing ...).

daily.title: Watching your roommate
daily.description: Your roommate is in a great mood, and you guess why.
daily.example: You're humming, so the date must have gone well, huh?

daily.title: Reading a mystery novel
daily.description: A detective reasons from clues at the scene.
daily.example: Since the window is open, the culprit must have escaped this way.

daily.title: Watching your child eat
daily.description: A mother watches her child eat happily.
daily.example: Judging from how he ate everything, he must have been really hungry.

work.title: Reading a client's reaction
work.description: A salesperson judges a client's interest from their reaction.
work.example: Judging from how many questions they keep asking, the client seems quite interested.

work.title: Market analysis report
work.description: Guessing consumer trends from data.
work.example: Judging from the rise in purchases by young people, the advertising seems to be working.

etymology: 「ところ」 originally means “place”. Here it is a formal noun meaning “situation, appearance”. 「を見ると」 means “when you look at ...”. Together they mean “judging by looking at the situation”, which became a way to guess.

similar.title: 〜とみえる
similar.explanation: 「〜とみえる」 comes at the end of a sentence: “it seems ...”, as in 「よほど疲れたとみえる」. 「〜ところを見ると」 comes in the middle and first states the evidence for the guess.

similar.title: 〜からすると・〜からすれば
similar.explanation: 「〜からすると」 judges from a viewpoint or data and has a wider scope. 「〜ところを見ると」 is based on a concrete situation you see in front of you.

similar.title: 〜らしい
similar.explanation: 「〜らしい」 is the guess itself, often placed in the second part after 「〜ところを見ると」. The two are often used together.

meaning: Assumes a situation is true and reasons or judges from there: “if ...”, “supposing ...”.
connection: Plain form (nouns and na-adjectives can take だ) + としたら／とすれば／とすると

senses.label: Hypothetical condition
senses.meaning: Assumes something that hasn't happened or is contrary to fact. The second part is the speaker's guess, wish or question. Often used with 「もし」 or 「仮に」. It stresses the “supposing” more than 「〜たら」.
senses.connection: Plain form + としたら／とすれば (often with 「もし」 or 「仮に」)
examples: If you won the lottery, what would you do?
Supposing what he says is true, we're in serious trouble.
If I could have just one wish come true, I'd want to travel around the world.

senses.label: Reasoning from a premise
senses.meaning: Takes news you heard or the current situation as a premise and draws a conclusion: “if that's the case, then ...”. Often as 「〜だとしたら」 or 「〜だとすれば」.
senses.connection: Plain form + (だ)としたら／とすれば、〜はずだ／だろう
examples: If the meeting starts at three, we'll be late unless we leave now.
If that's true, we should take measures right away.

senses.label: At the start of a sentence
senses.meaning: 「だとしたら」, 「だとすれば」 and 「とすると」 can start a sentence to reason from what the other person said: “in that case”.
senses.connection: Start of sentence + だとしたら／だとすれば／とすると、〜
examples: “I heard that restaurant is closed today.” “In that case, let's go somewhere else.”

notes: 「〜としたら」 leans colloquial, 「〜とすれば」 leans written. The meaning is almost the same.
Don't confuse it with 「ようとしたら」 (just as I was about to ...), the conditional of 「〜(よ)うとする」.
The second part is usually a guess, judgment, question or wish. It is not normally a command.

daily.title: Imagining with friends
daily.description: Chatting about what you'd do if you could travel through time.
daily.example: If you could go back in time, when would you go back to?

daily.title: Planning an outing
daily.description: Discussing plans based on the weather forecast.
daily.example: If it rains tomorrow, the hike is off.

daily.title: Discussing a rumor
daily.description: You hear a friend is quitting their job.
daily.example: If he's really leaving the company, it'll be lonely around here.

work.title: Discussing risks in a meeting
work.description: Talking about the impact of a project delay.
work.example: If the delivery date slips by a week, there will be extra costs.

work.title: Research paper
work.description: A paper proposes a hypothesis and reasons from it.
work.example: If this hypothesis is correct, the conventional explanation needs to be reconsidered.

etymology: Formed from the quoting particle 「と」 plus 「したら」 and 「すれば」, the conditional forms of 「する」. 「〜とする」 means “to assume ...”, so with a conditional it means “if we assume ...”.

similar.title: 〜とすれば・〜としたら・〜とすると
similar.explanation: The same forms already learned at N3. At N2 the focus is more on written reasoning and connections like 「だとすれば」. The meaning is the same.

similar.title: 〜たら
similar.explanation: 「〜たら」 is a general conditional and can describe things that will certainly happen (「家に着いたら電話する」). 「〜としたら」 stresses an assumption and is not used for things that will certainly happen.

similar.title: 〜なら
similar.explanation: 「〜なら」 often picks up what someone said and gives advice, as in 「京都に行くなら、秋がいい」. 「〜としたら」 stresses reasoning from an assumed premise.

similar.title: 〜としても
similar.explanation: 「〜としても」 is a hypothetical concession: “even if ..., still ...”, with a result against expectations. 「〜としたら」 is a straightforward hypothetical condition.

title: 〜とは (definition / surprise)
meaning: (1) Introduces a word or concept and defines it: “... means ...”. (2) Shows surprise at something unexpected: “to think that ...!”.
connection: Noun + とは (definition); plain form + とは (surprise)

senses.label: Definition
senses.meaning: Introduces a word or concept and then gives its definition: “X is ...”, “by X we mean ...”. The second part is often 「〜のことだ」, 「〜という意味だ」, 「〜を指す」, or the question 「〜とは何か」.
senses.connection: Noun + とは + 〜のことだ／〜という意味だ／何か
examples: 「積ん読」 (tsundoku) means buying books and leaving them piled up without reading them.
Have you ever thought about what happiness is?
The SDGs are the Sustainable Development Goals.

senses.label: Surprise
senses.meaning: The speaker is surprised, moved or indignant at something unexpected: “to think that ...”. Often 「〜とは思わなかった」 or 「〜とは驚いた」. The rest can also be dropped, ending with 「〜とは。」.
senses.connection: Plain form + とは (思わなかった／驚いた／。)
examples: I never imagined he was the culprit.
I'm amazed that you ate it all by yourself.
To think I'd run into an old friend in a place like this!

notes: The definition use is rather formal. In speech, 「〜って」 or 「〜というのは」 is more common.
The surprise use often goes with adverbs like 「まさか」 or 「こんなに」. Dropping the rest of the sentence leaves a stronger lingering effect.
Patterns like 「〜とは限らない」, 「〜とはいえ」 and 「〜とは言えない」 are different grammar points, not this usage.

daily.title: Hearing surprising news
daily.description: You're amazed to hear that friends are suddenly getting married.
daily.example: I never dreamed those two would get married!

daily.title: Looking up a word
daily.description: A student looks up a new word.
daily.example: 「ググる」 means to search on Google.

daily.title: Watching the news
daily.description: The news reports unusual weather.
daily.example: Snow in April? Strange things do happen.

work.title: Employee training
work.description: An instructor explains a technical term to new employees.
work.example: Compliance means following laws and the rules of society.

work.title: Academic paper
work.description: A paper defines its subject at the beginning.
work.example: In this paper, “young people” refers to those aged eighteen to twenty-nine.

etymology: Formed from the quoting particle 「と」 plus the topic particle 「は」. 「と」 presents the preceding content as something quoted, and 「は」 makes it the topic, giving the definition use “what is called ...”. Raising something unexpected as the topic and leaving the rest unsaid produced the tone of surprise.

similar.title: 〜というのは
similar.explanation: 「〜というのは」 has the same meaning as the definition use but is more colloquial. 「〜とは」 is more concise and formal.

similar.title: 〜とは (surprise)
similar.explanation: At N1, the surprise use is studied on its own, often in writing with the rest of the sentence dropped. This grammar point covers both basic uses: definition and surprise.

similar.title: 〜って (quoting / topic)
similar.explanation: 「〜って」 is the colloquial way to raise a topic or ask what something means, as in 「『積ん読』って何？」. It is the spoken equivalent of 「〜とは」.

meaning: Reports news or a message heard from someone else: “I hear that ...”, “I'm told that ...”.
connection: Plain form／imperative or volitional form, etc. + とのことだ (polite: 〜とのことです)

senses.label: Reporting what you heard
senses.meaning: Passes on words or news heard from someone else. Mostly used in letters, emails, business conversations and other formal settings. More formal than 「〜そうだ」, and the source is often stated with 「〜によると」 or 「〜から」.
senses.connection: Plain form + とのことだ／とのことです
examples: According to the weather forecast, there will be heavy snow tomorrow.
I'm told the department manager will be coming in late today.
Mr. Tanaka got in touch and said he can't attend the meeting.

senses.label: Passing on a message
senses.meaning: Passes on a message someone asked you to deliver, including requests, instructions or invitations. It can follow 「〜てほしい」, 「〜てください」 or 「〜ように」. Common in business when relaying what a boss or client wants.
senses.connection: 〜てほしい／〜ように／〜てください + とのことです
examples: The president says everyone should submit their reports by tomorrow.
My teacher asked me to give you his regards.

notes: 「だ」 is often dropped after 「とのこと」, ending with 「〜とのこと。」. This is common in emails and notices.
「〜とのことで」 can link clauses: “since I heard that ...”.
Not used to report things about yourself. For casual reporting in speech, 「〜って」 or 「〜そうだ」 is more common.

daily.title: Passing on a message to family
daily.description: A mother passes on Grandma's message to her child.
daily.example: Grandma says she'd like you to come visit this Sunday.

daily.title: Writing a letter
daily.description: In a letter, you mention news about a mutual friend.
daily.example: I was relieved to hear that Mr. Yamada is doing well too.

work.title: Relaying a phone call
work.description: A secretary tells the boss about a client's call.
work.example: Mr. Suzuki from Company A called and asked if you could call him back.

work.title: Business email
work.description: Reporting the other party's decision in an email.
work.example: We have been informed that they will revise their prices starting next month.

work.title: News and announcements
work.description: A station announcement relays a notice from the railway company.
work.example: Service is expected to resume at around 3 p.m.

etymology: Made of the quoting particle 「と」, the linking particle 「の」 and the noun 「こと」, plus the copula 「だ」. Literally “it is a matter of ...”, it presents what you heard as one “matter” to pass on.

similar.title: 〜そうだ (hearsay)
similar.explanation: 「〜そうだ」 is the general hearsay expression, used in speech and writing. 「〜とのことだ」 is more formal and often relays a specific message or piece of business.

similar.title: 〜ということだ (hearsay / conclusion)
similar.explanation: 「〜ということだ」 also reports hearsay, and can also state a conclusion (“in other words”). 「〜とのことだ」 is used only for reporting and sounds more formal.

similar.title: 〜との (quoting, before a noun)
similar.explanation: 「〜との + noun」, as in 「中止との連絡」 (a notice that it's canceled), modifies a noun to show its content. 「〜とのことだ」 reports at the end of a sentence.
